name: Leg press
angleNote: Knee flexion: 10° = legs nearly straight, 110° = sled lowered deep. Lifting makes the angle smaller. Torques are per leg.

strength.note: Relative hip-extension torque vs hip flexion, assumed strongest with the hip bent. Peak is per leg, typical trained adult. Approximate.
strength.source: TODO: verify against published torque–angle data

strength.note: Relative knee-extension torque vs knee flexion, weakest near straight, strongest around 60°. Peak is per leg. Approximate.
strength.source: TODO: verify against published torque–angle data

strength.note: Relative plantarflexion torque, strongest with the calf stretched. Peak is per leg. Approximate.
strength.source: TODO: verify against published torque–angle data

muscles.name: Quadriceps
muscles.note: Knee extensors: their share follows the knee torque.

muscles.name: Adductor magnus
muscles.note: Rear part extends the hip, more so when it is deeply bent.

muscles.name: Calves (soleus, gastrocnemius)
muscles.note: Plantarflexors: keep the shin from tipping forward.

phases.name: Top
phases.text: Legs nearly straight: the sled's line of push passes close to the knees.

phases.name: Bottom
phases.text: Deep: the knees and hips have their largest moment arms.

variants.name: 45° leg press, feet in the middle
variants.notes: The plate pushes along the rail. With the feet in the middle the push line runs close to the hip, so the knees do most of the work. Sled weight and friction are ignored (only the plates count).

variants.name: 45° leg press, feet high
variants.notes: Feet higher on the plate move the push line away from the hip and closer to the knee: more hip work, less knee work.

variants.name: 45° leg press, feet low
variants.notes: Feet low on the plate move the push line further from the knee: more knee work, and more ankle range.
